hints: Count the carbons in the benzene ring separately from the three carbons in the isopropyl group, then recall the geometry and bonding of each type.
walkthrough:
Separate ring carbons from side chain carbons**
Look at Fig. 5.1. Cumene is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2$. There are 6 carbons in the benzene ring and 3 carbons in the $\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2$ group, 9 carbons in total.

Assign hybridisation by bonding**
Each benzene carbon forms 3 sigma bonds in a trigonal planar arrangement with one p orbital left for the pi system, so all 6 are $\text{sp}^2$. Each side chain carbon forms 4 sigma bonds tetrahedrally with no pi bond, so all 3 are $\text{sp}^3$.
Final answer: $\text{sp}^2 = 6$ and $\text{sp}^3 = 3$

hints: Think about what species attacks the benzene ring in Fig. 5.2 and what part of benzene acts as the nucleophile.
walkthrough:
Recognise the benzene pattern**
Benzene is electron rich because of its delocalised pi system, so it is attacked by an electrophile, the $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH}^+$ cation. The $\text{H}$ on the ring is then substituted by the alkyl group, so the overall type is electrophilic substitution.

hints: Recall which Lewis acid catalyst is used to polarise a C-Br bond in a bromoalkane to generate a carbocation in Friedel-Crafts reactions.
walkthrough:
Link bromoalkane to catalyst**
To make $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH}^+$ from $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHBr}$, you need a strong Lewis acid that accepts the bromide. For chloroalkanes it is $\text{AlCl}_3$, so for bromoalkanes the matching carrier is $\text{AlBr}_3$. It polarises the $\text{C-Br}$ bond to release the carbocation electrophile.

hints: Start from the benzene pi system and think where the first curly arrow must come from to attack the positively charged carbon of $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH}^+$.
Recall what the intermediate looks like after one ring carbon becomes tetrahedral, with the positive charge delocalised around the ring.
Think how aromaticity is restored by removing the hydrogen from the same carbon that was attacked, and what small ion is lost.
walkthrough:
Make the first bond with the electrophile**
Picture benzene donating a pair of pi electrons. Draw a curly arrow starting inside the hexagon and pointing to the positively charged carbon of $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH}^+$. This forms a new $\text{C-C}$ bond between the ring and the isopropyl carbon.

Draw the Wheland intermediate correctly**
One ring carbon is now tetrahedral, bonded to H and to $\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2$, and the ring positive charge is delocalised over the other five carbons. Show the intermediate with a $+$ in the ring and the $\text{H}$ still attached at the site of attack. Aromaticity is temporarily lost.

Restore aromaticity by losing a proton**
Draw a curly arrow from the $\text{C-H}$ bond at the attacked carbon back into the ring to reform the pi system. The products are cumene plus $\text{H}^+$. Label the $+$ on the leaving $\text{H}^+$ clearly.

Final answer: Curly arrow from benzene pi system inside hexagon to $\text{C}^+$ of $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH}^+$ to give arenium intermediate with $+$ charge delocalised in ring and isopropyl group attached. Then curly arrow from $\text{C-H}$ bond at that carbon back into ring to reform aromatic pi system, losing $\text{H}^+$.

hints: Compare the number of alkyl groups attached to the positively charged carbon in $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2^+$ and in $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH}^+$.
walkthrough:
Classify and compare stabilisation**
$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2^+$ has the $\text{C}^+$ joined to only one alkyl group, so it is primary. $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH}^+$ has the $\text{C}^+$ joined to two alkyl groups, so it is secondary. Alkyl groups push electron density toward $\text{C}^+$ by the positive inductive effect, spreading the charge. More alkyl groups means more stabilisation, so rearrangement by hydride shift to the secondary cation is favoured.

Final answer: $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH}^+$ is a $2^\circ$ carbocation which is more stable than the $1^\circ$ $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2^+$ cation due to greater positive inductive effect from two alkyl groups.

hints: Write the expression $\Delta S^\ominus = \Sigma S^\ominus(\text{products}) - \Sigma S^\ominus(\text{reactants})$ and identify which two compounds are products and which two are reactants in reaction 1.
walkthrough:
Apply products minus reactants**
For reaction 1: $$\Delta S^\ominus = [S^\ominus(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH}) + S^\ominus(\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3)] - [S^\ominus(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2) + S^\ominus(\text{O}_2)]$$ Substitute from Table 5.2: $$\Delta S^\ominus = (146 + 200) - (278 + 205) = -137 \text{ J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}$$ The negative sign makes sense because a gas, $\text{O}_2$, is consumed.
Final answer: $\Delta S^\ominus = 146 + 200 - 205 - 278 = -137 \text{ J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}$

hints: Recall the equation linking $\Delta G^\ominus$, $\Delta H^\ominus$ and $\Delta S^\ominus$, and convert $25^\circ\text{C}$ to kelvin.
Check the units of $\Delta S^\ominus$ before substituting, then consider what the sign of the calculated $\Delta G^\ominus$ tells you about feasibility.
walkthrough:
Set up Gibbs equation with correct T**
Use: $$\Delta G^\ominus = \Delta H^\ominus - T\Delta S^\ominus$$ $T = 25 + 273 = 298 \text{ K}$. Convert $\Delta S^\ominus = -137 \text{ J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1} = -0.137 \text{ kJ K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}$ to match $\Delta H^\ominus$ in $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.

Calculate and conclude**
$$\Delta G^\ominus = -371 - (298 \times -0.137) = -371 + 40.8 = -330 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$ Because $\Delta G^\ominus < 0$, reaction 1 is feasible at $25^\circ\text{C}$.

Final answer: $\Delta G^\ominus = \Delta H^\ominus - T\Delta S^\ominus$ with $T = 298 \text{ K}$
$\Delta G^\ominus = -371 - 298 \times (-0.137) = -330 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$, negative so feasible.

hints: Recall the simple room temperature reagent for phenol bromination compared with the need for a halogen carrier and anhydrous conditions for benzene.
Focus on the oxygen atom in $\text{-OH}$ and what its lone pair can do with the benzene pi system.
Think how that interaction changes the electron density in the ring and its attraction for electrophiles.
Link the increased ring electron density to the ability to polarise a neutral $\text{Br}_2$ molecule without a catalyst.
walkthrough:
State the milder conditions**
For phenol use aqueous $\text{Br}_2$, bromine water, at room temperature. No Lewis acid catalyst such as $\text{AlBr}_3$ or $\text{FeBr}_3$ and no anhydrous conditions are needed, unlike benzene which needs $\text{Br}_2$ with $\text{FeBr}_3$ / $\text{AlBr}_3$.

Show the lone pair effect**
The key difference is the $\text{-OH}$ group. Oxygen has a lone pair in a p-orbital that can overlap with the delocalised pi system of the ring. This delocalisation pushes extra electron density into the ring.

Explain higher reactivity**
With more electron density, the ring attracts electrophiles more strongly. It is electron rich enough to induce a dipole in a neutral $\text{Br}_2$ molecule and polarise the $\text{Br-Br}$ bond itself, so no external catalyst is required to generate $\text{Br}^+$.

Contrast with benzene**
Benzene has no activating group, so its pi system alone cannot polarise $\text{Br}_2$ sufficiently. It needs $\text{FeBr}_3$ to create a stronger electrophile. Phenol is activated, so reaction is much faster and gives multiple substitution.

Final answer: Conditions: aqueous bromine / bromine water at room temperature, no $\text{AlBr}_3$ / $\text{FeBr}_3$ needed.
Lone pair / p-orbital on O overlaps and delocalises with ring pi system. Electron density in ring increases so ring is more attractive to electrophiles and polarises $\text{Br}_2$ more readily, so phenol is more reactive than benzene.

hints: Remember that the $\text{-OH}$ group is strongly 2,4,6 directing and that bromine water with phenol gives a white precipitate of the fully substituted product.
walkthrough:
Place three bromines ortho and para to OH**
Because $\text{-OH}$ activates ortho (2,6) and para (4) positions, all three react with excess aqueous $\text{Br}_2$. Draw phenol with $\text{Br}$ atoms at both positions next to $\text{OH}$ and one opposite $\text{OH}$. That is 2,4,6-tribromophenol.
Final answer: Q is 2,4,6-tribromophenol, benzene ring with $\text{OH}$ at position 1 and $\text{Br}$ at 2,4,6 positions.

hints: Look at product S in Fig. 5.4, it contains a $\text{-N=N-}$ link between two rings, so think what electrophile couples with phenol in NaOH(aq).
walkthrough:
Work backwards from the azo product**
S is an azo compound with a $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{N=N-}$ unit joined to phenol. The standard way to make this is coupling of phenol in $\text{NaOH(aq)}$ with a diazonium ion. So R must be benzenediazonium chloride, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}_2^+\text{Cl}^-$.
Final answer: R = $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}_2^+$ / $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{N}^+\equiv\text{N}$ / benzenediazonium chloride

hints: Name the $\text{-N=N-}$ linkage that joins the two aromatic rings in dye S.
walkthrough:
Name the N=N link**
The $\text{-N=N-}$ group joining two aryl groups in reaction 3 is the azo group, characteristic of azo dyes.

hints: Draw the monosubstituted phenol isomers with formula $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NO}_3$ and focus on positions relative to $\text{-OH}$.
Recall whether $\text{-OH}$ is an electron donating activating group and which positions it directs new electrophiles to.
walkthrough:
Draw the two major mononitro products**
Nitration replaces one ring H with $\text{NO}_2$. Draw phenol with $\text{NO}_2$ ortho to $\text{OH}$ for 2-nitrophenol (isomer 1) and para to $\text{OH}$ for 4-nitrophenol (isomer 2). The 3-isomer (meta) is formed in much smaller amount.

Justify with directing effect**
The $\text{-OH}$ group donates electron density into the ring by lone pair delocalisation, activating ortho and para positions. The electrophile $\text{NO}_2^+$ therefore attacks mainly at C2 and C4, giving the 2- and 4-isomers as major products.

Final answer: 2-nitrophenol and 4-nitrophenol.
$\text{-OH}$ is electron donating / activating and 2,4-directing (ortho and para directing), so substitution at 2 and 4 positions is favoured.
